content: The energy intakes observed in each dataset did not align with the fixed energy levels we used in our modeling, which were based on the estimated energy requirements (EERs) (refer to Annex 1). In our scenarios, we assumed that energy intakes would meet the EERs. Additionally, we assumed a fixed percentage of energy derived from breast milk for each age group, consistent with the modeling approach. Using these fixed breast milk intakes and EERs, we calculated the energy available for complementary foods and beverages (referred to as CF). We adjusted the intake patterns (percentages of energy from food groups and subgroups) to match those observed in the datasets, but the quantities (in grams and kilocalories) were modified to ensure that the total energy intake equaled the EER. For our optimization modeling, we used three energy levels (low, middle, and high) for each age group in the initial modeling of best-case scenarios (details in Annex 1). For the scenarios described here, we selected one energy level for each country setting. We considered body weight data available in the datasets and the nutritional context of each country. Table 2 provides data on anthropometric indicators at the national level for the three countries. For Bangladesh and Malawi, we selected EERs based on low body weights. For Mexico, we selected EERs based on average body weights. Once the EERs were determined, we calculated the grams per food subgroup for each dataset and age/feeding group in each setting as follows: 1. Energy intake from excluded items was subtracted from the total energy derived from CF (details of excluded items are in Annex 3). Note that both breast milk and infant formula were excluded at this stage. 2. We summed the energy from all non-excluded food groups and subgroups to calculate the total CF kilocalories. 3. We calculated the percentage of energy for each food subgroup as: (Mean energy (kcal) for the food subgroup ÷ Total CF kilocalories) × 100. 4. We calculated the percentage of energy from the five broad food groups by summing the percentages of their respective subgroups. 5. We back-calculated kilocalories for each subgroup as: (Available CF kilocalories × Percentage of kilocalories from each subgroup) ÷ 100. 6. We calculated grams per food subgroup as: (Kilocalories per subgroup × 100) ÷ Kilocalories per 100 grams of the subgroup in the nutrient profile. These gram amounts were then used to calculate the nutrients in the food patterns and the percentage of the Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) for each nutrient. It is important to note that this procedure redistributed the energy from excluded items proportionately across all other food subgroups. While this approach may not always be justified, we had no alternative basis for redistribution. The nature of the excluded items varied by country and, to some extent, by age group within countries. In Bangladesh, nearly all excluded items were added sugars. In Malawi, the most commonly excluded items were sugar (by far the most common), broth, and plain tea. In Mexico, the most common excluded items (aside from salt and water) were garlic, sugar, and soup broth. By redistributing the kilocalories from these excluded items proportionately across the other food groups, the food patterns were slightly improved but remained impoverished in Bangladesh and Malawi, with very high percentages of energy derived from starchy staple foods. The Mexican food pattern was somewhat better. It should be noted that our data for food subgroup consumption were averaged across breastfed and non-breastfed infants and young children (IYC), implicitly assuming that patterns were similar between the two feeding groups after excluding breast milk and formula. This assumption was made because, in many settings, subgroup sample sizes based on milk feeding status would have been too small for analysis. However, it is possible that food patterns differ between these groups. Therefore, in most cases, we restricted our scenarios to those where this assumption was less significant. In Bangladesh and Malawi, nearly all IYC were breastfed, so we created scenarios for breastfed IYC. In Mexico, feeding practices were more mixed during infancy. Nevertheless, we created a scenario for breastfed infants, assuming that patterns would be similar across feeding groups, though this assumption may not be valid. For 9-month-old children in Mexico, only 14% were breastfed, so we created a scenario for non-breastfed children only. Despite these limitations, we hope the scenarios will serve as useful examples of broad patterns with some basis in real-world settings. Blank cells in the data tables indicate that the food subgroup was not consumed by at least 5% of the IYC.
